Goldman: Outside of the very short-term trading pattern around the IPO, SpaceX has had a much smaller impact on equity indices than many investors expected. 

Among major US equity indices, SpaceX carries the largest weight within the Nasdaq-100. Excluding SpaceX, the P/E of the Nasdaq-100 would be less than half a turn lower than its current multiple. Furthermore, the inclusion of SpaceX has not had a major effect on the Nasdaq-100 index return, volatility, or concentration. 

Coincidentally, the limited fundamental impact of SpaceX index inclusion has been reminiscent of Tesla's 2020 inclusion in the S&P 500, when the stock had only a minor impact on index valuation.

Late Friday we got the Fed's US consumer credit report for September which showed a jump of $27.84 billion, the most since November 2022. That’s about double the $13.80 billion expected and above every estimate in Bloomberg’s survey with both revolving (mostly credit cards) and nonrevolving debt seeing double-digit increases.

▪️ Revolving (mostly credit cards) rose $16.30 billion (+14.46% annualized), the most since November 2023. That came a month after August’s drop, which was revised down to $4.97 billion and was the biggest decline since November 2024.
▪️ Nonrevolving (mostly student and auto loans) rose $11.54 billion. That brings its three-month total to $39.63 billion, the most since December 2022.
▪️ All three measures are at record highs: total $5.224 trillion, revolving $1.368 trillion and nonrevolving $3.856 trillion.
▪️ Year-over-year, revolving is up 4.25%, the fastest since October 2024. Total is up 3.01% and nonrevolving 2.57%.
▪️ The Fed’s quarterly detail shows student loans ($1.885 trillion) and auto loans ($1.590 trillion) both at records at the end of September.
▪️ The rate on credit card accounts assessed interest rose to 22.36% in the third quarter, the highest since August 2025, from 22.15%.

Bloomberg frames this as consumers leaning on cards because real pay is lagging prices. Hourly earnings are up 3.12% from a year ago, while September CPI was 3.7%.

But zooming out after inflation (September CPI 3.7%), total consumer credit is down 0.69% from a year ago, the seventh straight month below zero, and card balances are up only about half a point, versus more than 8% in late 2022. August and September together added $11.33 billion in card balances, or $5.67 billion a month. That’s only a bit above the past year’s $4.64 billion monthly average, so September is more catch-up. 

Also keep in mind these are balances at a single point in time during the monthly cycle, and much of them gets paid off before any interest is charged.

Goldman’s latest update notes that through Thursday US Fundamental Long/Short (L/S) Gross leverage fell 8.7 pts – the largest weekly decline since Covid (March ’20) – to the 26th percentile one-year, while US Fundamental L/S Net leverage fell 3.7 pts – the largest weekly decline since the week of liberation day (Apr ’25) – back down to the 0th percentile five-year.

And while last week I had noted that the beta-adjusted figures were much higher (beta-adjusted net leverage was 63.9%, only at the 41st percentile over three years and the 53rd over five, vs. the 5th for raw net), meaning there was more risk in hedge fund books than it appeared, those dropped sharply to 57.4% (−6.4 pts), the 0th percentile one-year, the 4th over three years and the 22nd over five. 

Beta-adjusted gross fell even more, down 15.7 pts to 213.2%, the 0th percentile one-year and the 5th over three years (from the 69th). 

Back of the envelope, their longs’ average beta slipped to about 1.08 from 1.11, meaning they mostly sold their highest-beta longs (AI/semis). The hidden risk finally came out of the books.

While the election was the most recent catalyst, as @sonusvarghese notes (via @dailychartbook’s nightly email), the rotation out of AI has been going on for a while now, with the six-month return gap between Goldman’s Broad AI index and its S&P 500 ex-AI index plunging to around -35 percentage points. 

That’s the worst reading of the four-year bull market by a wide margin. It’s nearly three times as bad as the roughly -10-point trough after the DeepSeek shock and the tariff selloff in early 2025, and the roughly -12-point low during the summer 2024 rotation and yen carry-trade unwind. It’s also a swing of roughly 100 points from the +67 peak in September 2025.
